overview: Saudi Arabia is the kingdom proclaimed in 1932, joining regions with different urban, farming and pastoral histories. This imported record begins in 1938. Its first outline wrongly includes Sana’a in Yemen, while all six snapshots omit Dammam. Available polygons end at 2020 even though the index continues to the present. Those map defects are not political events, and the older Nejd and Hejaz records remain separate.

periods.title: Oil and expanding institutions
periods.summary: Commercial oil production and growing state ownership transformed the kingdom’s economy during these mapped decades.

periods.title: Basic Law and continuing change
periods.summary: The Basic Law formalized royal institutions; the kingdom continues through social and economic changes.

sections.title: A kingdom, discoveries and global influence

items.text: The Basic Law issued in 1992 describes an Islamic monarchy, with succession among the founder Abdulaziz’s sons and descendants. The king supervises general policy and commands the armed forces. Royal institutions hold extensive authority; this is not a system in which voters elect the national ruler.

A 1933 concession brought American oil exploration to the Eastern Province. After difficult early drilling, Dammam No. 7 began commercial production in 1938. Geologists searched for promising sites while drilling crews tested them. The oil industry began with investigation and repeated setbacks, not a ready-made fountain of wealth.

Saudi guide Khamis ibn Rimthan helped exploration teams navigate unfamiliar desert country. Aramco’s historical account describes him leading large camel caravans by the early 1940s, when motor transport was still limited. Knowledge of routes and terrain mattered alongside geological instruments: an expedition needed to reach its destination before it could investigate it.

The 1,212-kilometre Trans-Arabian Pipeline, completed in 1950, connected eastern Saudi oilfields with the Mediterranean export route. In 1980 the Saudi government increased its ownership of Aramco to 100 percent. Transport infrastructure and ownership changed together as oil became a much larger source of state power.

Saudi Arabia was one of five states that founded OPEC at Baghdad in September 1960, alongside Iran, Iraq, Kuwait and Venezuela. Abdullah al-Tariki represented Saudi Arabia among the founders. The organization gave oil-producing governments a forum for coordinating policies that affected customers far beyond the region.

During the 1973 Arab-Israeli War, Saudi Arabia and other participating Arab oil exporters restricted supplies to the United States and other supporters of Israel. The embargo contributed to a wider energy crisis and intense diplomacy before it was lifted in March 1974. Oil prices also reflected other economic pressures; one decision did not explain the whole crisis.

In Asir, women traditionally decorate guest-room walls with al-Qatt al-Asiri painting. Female relatives of different ages help, drawing geometric forms and symbols on a usually white gypsum base. Children can learn by watching and practising alongside older relatives. Here the family artwork can be an entire wall, not just a drawing attached to the refrigerator.

Arabic coffee is part of hospitality in Saudi Arabia and neighbouring countries. UNESCO’s account describes serving elders and guests first, sharing poetry and conversation, and shaking the cup to signal that one has finished. A small movement saves a long explanation: the cup has its own polite vocabulary.

Al-Ahsa’s oasis is a working landscape of springs, wells, open canals, gardens and settlements. Water distribution links farms to one another, and drainage is part of the system too. Its agricultural history long predates the modern kingdom. The greenery is the result of sustained work with water, rather than the desert simply deciding to become a garden.

UNESCO’s Al-Ahsa listing describes about 2.5 million date palms, but dates are not the only crop. A local red rice variety also survives. Historic souks and modern markets distribute farm produce and handicrafts. An oasis meal and a market basket can therefore reveal more variety than a picture of palms alone suggests.

Historic Jeddah preserves late nineteenth-century merchant tower houses built before the Saudi kingdom. Ground floors could serve business, while rooms accommodated pilgrims travelling to Mecca. Such buildings brought work, lodging and household life under one roof. The city’s Red Sea connections carried people, food and ideas from Africa and Asia.

Jeddah’s wooden roshan projections create shaded extensions to living rooms. The nomination describes people sitting or sleeping there and placing clay water pots in the shade and airflow. Louvred panels admitted breezes. A window could be a small living space as well as an opening to look through.

King Saud University was established in 1957. Its institutional history records an initial Arts intake of twenty-one male students. Women began entering in 1381 AH, approximately 1961 to 1962; the first group in English comprised four Saudi women. These small cohorts put human scale on the expansion of university education.

Building a public girls’ school system also required teachers. The King Saud Library records a women’s teacher-training institute in 1380 AH and fifteen girls’ primary schools in the 1380 to 1381 academic year, around 1960 to 1962. These were milestones in public schooling, not the beginning of all learning among Saudi girls.

WHO validated Saudi Arabia’s elimination of trachoma as a public health problem in January 2022. Trachoma can damage sight. The achievement involved connecting eye care with local health services and cooperation with education, water and agriculture authorities. The precise milestone matters: it did not mean that no future patient could ever develop the disease.

The ban on women driving ended on 24 June 2018, a change welcomed by the UN Secretary-General. Yet Human Rights Watch had reported the arrest of women’s-rights campaigners the previous month, including Eman al-Nafjan and Loujain al-Hathloul. New opportunities and repression occurred in the same period; the reform did not erase the campaigners’ experiences.

SAMA’s Arabic announcement dated 4 October 2020 contains “خمسة ريالات”, transliterated khamsat riyālāt, meaning “five riyals”. This is a short modern Arabic writing sample from the announcement’s first paragraph, with its meaning confirmed by the parallel English version. It identifies the denomination of a new banknote; it is not an ancient inscription.

The new five-riyal note was made of polymer and scheduled to circulate from 5 October 2020 alongside cotton notes. Its front showed King Salman and the Shaybah oilfield, while the back showed wildflowers. A transparent window carried decorative motifs. Everyday money put petroleum and small desert flowers in the same pocket.

ending.text: Saudi Arabia continues as a kingdom. The last available map snapshot is not a fall date. Royal institutions and distinctive regional communities have continued through extensive economic and social change.
